before: Inside a function, := is a short variable declaration. In the same block it needs at least one new non-blank name.
A new score declared inside braces is distinct from an outer score. Updating that inner object does not update the outer one.
= assigns an existing name instead of declaring a new one. Scope determines which existing variable is selected.
Similar spelling is not proof of the same object. Read the block boundaries and declaration operator.

Expected output or behavior: 7
3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Draw the scopes and compare a declaration with an assignment. Explain why a repeated name alone is ambiguous. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Scope is the part of the code where a name is available. Braces create a block with its own scope. Inside a function, `:=` declares names; at least one must be new in that block, excluding the discard name `_`.
An inner block can declare its own score. This hides the outer score inside that block, but the two variables remain separate.
`=` assigns a value to an existing variable. It does not create a new variable.
To find which score a line uses, look at its surrounding braces. Then check whether the line declares a new name or updates an existing one.
The screen shows `7`, then `3`. The first line reads the inner score. After the inner block ends, the second line reads the outer score.
Replace the inner `:=` with `=`. There is then no new inner score; the assignment changes the outer variable.
